q.young: Does your tummy hurt more when you walk or jump?
q.older: Does the pain get worse when you walk, jump, or cough?

candidates.why: Top-ranked item: the strongest history variable in the best-performing model (pARC), and nothing else the app collects can stand in for it. Asks what the child already noticed, never asks them to hop.

review.reason: pARC treats walk/jump/cough as ONE variable, any manoeuvre counting; kept all three so a child in a bed who cannot walk or jump can still answer via cough

q.young: Does it hurt more when you cough?
q.older: Does coughing make your tummy hurt more?

candidates.why: Alternate wording for item 5, narrowed to the coughing half. Offered because the three-verb version is a compound yes/no; a reviewer may prefer the single, unambiguous verb. Only one item-5 question ships.

review.reason: cough-only alternate: narrows a single three-manoeuvre criterion and makes it unanswerable for a child who can only cough

q.young: Did you throw up?
q.older: Have you thrown up since your tummy started hurting?

candidates.why: Commonest associated symptom at 58% and named by six sources; also the re-sourced replacement for the hand-written `threw-up` follow-up, which is dropped once the bank covers tummy.

review.reason: matches the wording the app already ships, so nothing is lost in the handover

q.young: Did it start hurting in a different place first?
q.older: Did the pain start somewhere else before it moved to where it is now?

candidates.why: Migration is in every prediction rule, and the body map already supplies where it is now, so only the whether half is missing. Asks whether, never where; the nurse maps the pair.

review.reason: clearer than t-005

q.young: Was the hurt somewhere else when it started?
q.older: Was the pain in a different spot when it first began?

candidates.why: Alternate wording for item 4, avoiding the word moved in case a child reads it as being asked to point. Only one item-4 question ships.

review.reason: alternate; t-004 is clearer

q.young: Does it hurt when you pee?
q.older: Does it hurt or sting when you pee?

candidates.why: UTI is 5% of these children and is invisible to every appendicitis score in the packet; the app currently asks a child with a sore tummy nothing about weeing.

review.reason: direct; t-007's construction is odd

q.young: Does peeing feel stingy?
q.older: Have you had any stinging when you pee?

candidates.why: Alternate wording for item 12 leading with the sensation rather than the word hurt, which the FPS-R screen has already used heavily by this point. Only one item-12 question ships.

review.reason: alternate; 'does peeing feel stingy' is awkward

q.young: Does it hurt more now than before?
q.older: Is the pain worse now than when it started?

candidates.why: A trajectory rather than a snapshot, and the only item the packet keeps in the long-time band; also the question a repeat visit exists to answer.

review.reason: band-agnostic

q.young: Is it hurting more and more?
q.older: Has the pain been getting worse as the day goes on?

candidates.why: Alternate wording for item 7 that captures progression rather than a two-point comparison, which matters most in the long-time band where there is no clear start point. Only one item-7 question ships.

review.reason: alternate; 'as the day goes on' breaks in the few-days band

q.young: Did you poop today?
q.older: Have you pooped today?

candidates.why: Constipation is 13% of diagnoses; re-sources the hand-written `bathroom-today` follow-up so it survives. Asks when, never whether the child is constipated, and carries no hint of fault.

review.reason: "have you pooped today?" accepted as sufficient

q.young: Did you poop yesterday?
q.older: Did you poop yesterday?

candidates.why: Alternate for item 10 that reaches back a day, since a no to today alone does not separate a normal morning from several days without. Only useful as the second step of a pair, which the yes/no-only screen cannot currently render; flagged for the reviewer.

review.reason: "have you pooped today?" is sufficient; the when-variant needs an answer type the app lacks

q.young: Has your poop been runny?
q.older: Has your poop been runny or watery?

candidates.why: Second commonest associated symptom at 28.9%, and gastroenteritis is 26% of diagnoses; no prediction rule contains it, so it exists only because source 6 is organised by complaint.

review.reason: accepted

q.young: Do you want to eat something?
q.older: Do you feel like eating anything right now?

candidates.why: Four sources name anorexia; a child cannot use that word but can say whether they feel like eating. Deliberately the appetite form rather than the shipped `ate-today`, which asks a different fact.

review.reason: accepted as yes/no; flag for the nurse that a nil-by-mouth child will answer this confusingly

q.young: Was there blood in your poop?
q.older: Have you seen any blood in your poop?

candidates.why: Something a child sees directly and can report; a red flag in three sources. Uses the plain observable word rather than any clinical description of stool.

review.reason: not shipped in v1 — same treatment as item 17. A yes/no naming blood is leading (yes is the escalating answer) and the packet's own cautions require a neutral colour widget the app does not have yet

q.young: Did you see blood in the toilet?
q.older: Have you seen any blood in the toilet after you poop?

candidates.why: Alternate for item 11 that points at the toilet rather than at the child's own body, which may be easier for a young child to answer without embarrassment. Only one item-11 question ships.

review.reason: not shipped in v1 — same treatment as item 17. A yes/no naming blood is leading (yes is the escalating answer) and the packet's own cautions require a neutral colour widget the app does not have yet

q.young: Are you drinking lots and peeing lots?
q.older: Have you been drinking more than usual and peeing more than usual?

candidates.why: Both halves of the polyuria/polydipsia pair in one question, as the packet directs; DKA presenting as tummy pain is a life-threatening miss no score here touches. Never names the condition.

review.reason: accepted

q.young: Is it hard to breathe, or do you have a cough?
q.older: Have you had a cough, or has it been hard to breathe?

candidates.why: Chest causes of tummy pain. Needs an id distinct from the chest group's `breathing` question and must not fire when the child has also tapped chest, since the pipeline dedupes by question id rather than by fact.

review.reason: split into two questions — see t-017a / t-017b

q.young: Did you swallow something that isn't food?
q.older: Have you swallowed anything that isn't food?

candidates.why: Time-critical, trivially reportable, and absent from every score; only the child or a witness knows. Names no object, so it cannot prompt or frighten the child into a denial.

review.reason: accepted

q.young: Do you feel hot?
q.older: Do you feel hot or shivery?

candidates.why: Captures the raw sensation and leaves the threshold to the nurse with the thermometer; three sources use three incompatible cutoffs. Never says fever and never asks for a number.

review.reason: accepted

q.young: Did your tummy hurt more when the car went over a bump?
q.older: On the way here, did the pain get worse when the car went over a bump?

candidates.why: Vivid and answerable, but the weakest provenance in the packet: one source, and that source is a protocol whose variables are being tested rather than validated. First to drop if the list must shrink.

review.reason: removed entirely: assumes the child arrived by car and was awake for it; a child brought by ambulance, on foot or asleep has no answer and yes/no offers no "didn't happen"

q.young: Does the hurt stop and then come back?
q.older: Does the pain go away for a while and then come back?

candidates.why: Colicky versus constant pain, which clinicians failed to document in 68% of cases, so a child's answer may be the only record. Ranks low: it overlaps SENSATIONS cramping, and young children conflate stopped with paused.

review.reason: accepted with minAge 7 — see meta

q.young: Does your tummy feel yucky, like you might throw up?
q.older: Do you feel like you might throw up, even though you haven't?

candidates.why: A genuinely separate variable in pARC, not a softer version of vomiting. Ranks last because SENSATIONS already offers queasy on the inside list before follow-ups are reached.

review.reason: SENSATIONS.queasy already covers nausea and item 2 ranks last, so it would never be selected; rejected to keep the bank lean

q.young: Is it hard to breathe?
q.older: Is it hard to breathe right now?

candidates.why: Breathing now. Split from the cough half so a yes is interpretable — the two have different time windows.

review.reason: split from the compound item-18 question

q.young: Have you had a cough or a cold?
q.older: Have you had a cough or a cold in the last two weeks?

candidates.why: Recent respiratory infection. SPASMS scopes this to two weeks; kept explicit for the older tier.

review.reason: split from the compound item-18 question
